eligibility_reason: The record's subject is agent memory that persists written content across sessions and is later recalled to condition behaviour: 'Malicious content encountered in one interaction may be stored in memory, persist after that interaction ends, and later be recalled to influence the agent's behavior' (p. 1). The evaluated systems (OpenClaw/Hermes agent harnesses paired with Native, Mem0, Mem0-Graph and A-MEM memory backends) write agent-facing state at run time via 'the intended agent-facing memory interface' and retrieve it in later sessions to affect subsequent actions (p. 2, Table 1 row IW/DC). It is 2026, English, and full text (29 pages) was retrievable, so I2-I4 hold. No E-criterion applies: it is not hardware/cache-only (E1), the store is externalised and agent-written, not parametric-only (E2), the agent writes to the store rather than retrieving from a fixed corpus (E3), it is a primary empirical benchmark, not a secondary/survey study (E4), memory is the explicit subject of the contribution, not incidental (E5), the systems under study are LLM-based agents (E6), and the paper is well over four pages with a full evaluation (E7).

facets.justification: The paper's own contribution is the comparison protocol, not any single store: 'The reported contrasts therefore compare complete memory-backend conditions, not isolated memory mechanisms' (p. 15, Appendix C). Four structurally different backends are evaluated with matched rigor and none is privileged as primary: OpenClaw-Native is file-based (MEMORY.md/USER.md/memory/*.md) with a derived SQLite hybrid index, Hermes-Native is two bounded in-context text stores injected at session start, Mem0 is a pgvector store, Mem0-Graph adds entity-linked rows in a Postgres table with 'no edge table, relation type, or multi-hop traversal', and A-MEM is a Chroma vector store of MemoryNote objects (pp. 15-16). Even the paper's own comparison anchor, 'Native', splits into two irreconcilable implementations (OpenClaw file store vs. Hermes bounded text store) depending on harness, so no single value can be picked without misrepresenting the design (pp. 15-16). Table 1's own dimension list names 'MMI: controlled comparison across memory backends' as a criterion the paper itself satisfies (p. 2), i.e. the multi-backend spread is deliberate, not an oversight.

Write mechanics differ by backend and the paper does not designate one as its contribution: OpenClaw-Native 'updates these files through ordinary file operations' with no stated transformation (p. 15); Mem0's standard path 'sets infer=false and directly stores the submitted text' with no transformation (p. 15); A-MEM's non-first adds instead invoke a memory-side model that performs 'content analysis, evolution, and constrained link or neighbor-metadata updates' (p. 16) -- a synthesis step absent from the other backends. Because the evaluation deliberately holds this dimension as an independent variable across matched conditions rather than arguing for one transformation, no single write_policy value is decidable from the given pages without guessing which backend is 'the' mechanism.

Retrieval differs by backend and, notably, even within 'Native': OpenClaw-Native uses a declared fusion rule ('Hybrid ranking uses semantic and lexical weights of 0.7 and 0.3', p. 15), while Hermes-Native 'has no query-time semantic retrieval' and instead 'injects a frozen system-prompt snapshot' at session start (p. 15) -- always-in-context, not hybrid. Mem0 and A-MEM retrieval is described as 'tool-driven rather than injected at session start' (pp. 15-16). With no backend held constant as the paper's own proposed mechanism, and the comparison across these differing policies being the explicit point of the study (Table 1, 'MMI', p. 2), no single retrieval_policy value can be assigned without fabricating a primary the paper does not designate.

Every case 'runs in an isolated Docker container with access only to benchmark-managed workspaces and service networks' (p. 16) under a controlled, matched-configuration protocol -- a novel benchmark investigated in the lab, not a system fielded for real users or with external stakes. No deployment or real-world usage is reported in the given pages.

310 fixed task cases are run across a 24-configuration matrix (2 harnesses x 4 memory backends x 3 LLM backends) and outcome rates are reported per configuration (MPSR, MESR, E2E-ASR, SRSR; Figures 10-11, pp. 27-28), matching a fixed task suite scored across systems. The design also holds conditions matched pairwise (p. 15, Appendix C intro), but the reported evidence is score-based over the fixed 310-case suite rather than a single manipulated-variable experiment.

The first listed contribution is the benchmark corpus itself: 'Memory Security Benchmark. We introduce MemSecBench, a task-grounded benchmark of 310 Write-Execute-Forget packages that trace malicious semantics through persistence, verified external consequence, and selective repair across seven evidence-based checkpoints' (p. 2).
